title: Guru ka Bagh, 1922
hookLine: volunteers took police beatings without striking back, and the world saw it

cards: Dry branches, an axe, and a kitchen fire that needs feeding. In a village outside Amritsar there's a gurdwara called Guru ka Bagh, the Guru's garden, with land around it where acacia trees grow.
Sikh volunteers go out to cut wood for the langar, the free kitchen. The custodian who holds the shrine says the land and the trees are his. The police arrest the woodcutters for theft.
And then more volunteers keep coming, walking toward the police lines with their hands at their sides.

teach.b: Like Nankana and Tarn Taran, Guru ka Bagh was in the hands of a mahant, a hereditary custodian, and the reformers said a Guru's shrine belonged to the whole panth. The wood was a small thing. Who owned the garden was not.
Jathas, groups of volunteers, set out each day from the Akal Takht in Amritsar, vowed to stay peaceful. At the garden the police met them with heavy sticks and beat them to the ground.
Accounts written at the time describe men falling, getting up, and being struck again, without raising a hand.
Charles Freer Andrews, an English clergyman, went to see for himself. He wrote that he watched the blows fall on men who did not strike back, and that the sight brought the crucifixion to his mind.
His account was printed and read far beyond Punjab, and that's how the world came to see it.
In the Asa di Var, at Ang 470 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak says sweetness and humility are the essence of every virtue and all goodness.
The volunteers walked to the garden humbly, with no weapon and no curse. But humble didn't mean bowed: when they were knocked down, they got up.
The week ran from Udham Singh and Bhagat Singh to the SGPC, Tarn Taran, Nankana and the keys, and it ends here.

how: Sikhs remember Guru ka Bagh as one of the peaceful campaigns of the gurdwara reform movement; the gurdwara near Amritsar keeps its memory, and the story is told in histories of the Akali movement.

practice: C. F. Andrews didn't march; he went, watched, and wrote down what he saw.
Bring to mind one time you saw someone stand firm while treated unfairly, and picture it plainly, adding nothing, then ask on the breath out: if I told this to one other person, what would I say?
If you pray, rest Waheguru on each breath.
